rtd_description: The Electrolyzer component is used to convert electrical energy into hydrogen gas through electrolysis in both centralized and decentralized configurations, producing hydrogen and waste heat. During operation, it takes electrical energy as its primary input and, through the splitting of water molecules using an electric current, converts it into hydrogen gas for the downstream system, while the waste heat can optionally be used via a connected heat bus. This process is mainly governed by the efficiency parameter, which defines the electricity-to-hydrogen conversion rate of the component, and by the recovered heat efficiency, which defines the usable share of the waste heat. Only electricity is modelled as input, so water costs are neglected, and the minimal operation level and standby consumption are not considered. \n\nSource of default parameter set: DEATechnikKatalogRenewableFuels - 08.26 - Alkaline Electrolysis (AEC) for 10 MW plant, ctrl. 2025

rtd_description: The recovered heat efficiency defines the share of the electrical input that can be used as heat, e.g. 0,1 means that 10 kWh of heat are recovered per 100 kWh of electricity. Electrolysers lose a considerable part of their input energy as low-temperature waste heat, which can be used e.g. for space heating or as a heat source for a heat pump, depending on its temperature level. The parameter only has an effect if a heat bus is connected, and together with the conversion efficiency it should not exceed 1.

rtd_description: The CHP Variable Ratio component is used to generate electrical and thermal energy simultaneously with a flexible power-to-heat ratio, as in extraction-condensing plants, so that the share of electricity and heat can be adjusted to the current demand. During operation, it takes a chemical energy source, such as natural gas, as its primary input and, through a combustion process with controllable heat extraction, converts it into electricity and usable heat, operating anywhere between full condensation mode, in which only electricity is produced, and maximum heat extraction mode, in which the highest heat output is achieved at the cost of a lower electricity output (power loss index, also known as beta coefficient). This process is mainly governed by the electrical efficiency parameters for both operating modes and the thermal efficiency parameter, which define the range within which the power-to-heat ratio can be varied. \n\nSource of default parameter set: DEATechnikKatalogelanddh - 08.26 - Gas turbine, combined cycle extraction, for one Unit - ctrl.2020

short_description: Enter the highest electrical efficiency the CHP can reach when minimizing heat extraction e.g. 0,45 for 45%
rtd_description: The electrical efficiency at minimum heat extraction represents the share of the fuel input converted into electricity when the plant operates under conditions that maximize electrical output. It is the highest electrical efficiency achievable by the plant. As heat extraction increases, electrical output decreases, a relationship described by the power loss index, also known as the beta coefficient. Together with the efficiencies at maximum heat extraction, it defines the operating range of the variable-ratio CHP.

verbose: Electrical efficiency at maximum heat extraction
short_description: Enter the minimum electrical efficiency of the CHP when maximum heat is extracted, e.g. 0,35 for 35%.
rtd_description: The minimum electrical efficiency is achieved at maximum heat extraction, when the plant prioritizes heat production over electricity generation. It represents the lowest share of fuel input converted into electricity and defines the lower limit of the CHP's electrical efficiency range.

verbose: Thermal efficiency  at minimum heat extraction
short_description: Enter the minimum thermal efficiency of the CHP, which is the amount of heat that always has to be used.
rtd_description: The minimum thermal efficiency is achieved at the operating point where electrical output is maximized and heat extraction is minimized. It represents the lowest share of fuel input converted into useful heat and, together with the maximum thermal efficiency, defines the range of thermal efficiencies within which the variable-ratio CHP can operate.

rtd_description: The maximum thermal efficiency is achieved at maximum heat extraction, when the plant prioritizes heat production. It represents the highest share of fuel input converted into useful heat and defines the upper limit of the CHP's thermal efficiency range.

rtd_description: The CHP Fixed Ratio component is used to generate electrical and thermal energy simultaneously in a fixed ratio, so that electricity and heat are always produced together and cannot be controlled independently. During operation, it takes a chemical energy source, such as natural gas or biogas, as its primary input and, through a combustion process in an engine coupled with heat recovery, converts it into electricity and usable heat, whereby every kWh of electricity is always accompanied by a fixed amount of heat, regardless of whether the unit follows the heat or the electricity demand. This process is mainly governed by the electrical and thermal efficiency parameters, which define the fixed fuel-to-electricity and fuel-to-heat conversion rates and thus the constant power-to-heat ratio of the component. \n\nSource of default parameter set: DEATechnikKatalogelanddh - 08.26 - Gas turbine, combined cycle back pressure, for one Unit - ctrl.2020

short_description: Enter the electrical efficiency of the CHP when heat is fully used, e.g. 0,35 for 35%.
rtd_description: The electrical efficiency describes how much of the fuel energy the CHP converts into electricity. As electricity and heat are always produced together in a fixed ratio, the electrical and thermal efficiency together determine how much electricity is produced per unit of heat: with an electrical efficiency of 0,35 and a thermal efficiency of 0,55, 1 kWh of natural gas results in 0,35 kWh of electricity and 0,55 kWh of heat, i.e. for every 100 kWh of heat, about 64 kWh of electricity are produced. This ratio applies in every hour, regardless of whether the CHP follows the heat or the electricity demand.

short_description: Enter the thermal efficiency of the CHP when heat is fully used, e.g. 0,55 for 55%.
rtd_description: The thermal efficiency describes how much of the fuel energy the CHP provides as usable heat, e.g. from the engine cooling and the exhaust gas or from the steam after the turbine. Together with the electrical efficiency, it defines the fixed ratio of the two outputs: with a thermal efficiency of 0,55 and an electrical efficiency of 0,35, 1 kWh of natural gas results in 0,55 kWh of heat and 0,35 kWh of electricity in every hour of operation.

rtd_description: The Heat Pump component is used to generate thermal energy for heating applications, such as space heating and domestic hot water. Unlike an electric heater, it does not convert electricity directly into heat, but uses it to transfer heat from a low-temperature source, such as outdoor air, groundwater or the ground, to a higher temperature level. During operation, it takes electrical energy as its primary input and, through a vapor compression cycle in which a refrigerant absorbs ambient heat while evaporating and releases it at a higher temperature after compression, converts it into usable heat output. This process is mainly governed by the coefficient of performance (COP) parameter, which defines the ratio of heat output to electricity input of the component; as the COP depends on the source and supply temperatures, it can also be given as a timeseries, e.g. calculated with oemof.thermal. \n\nSource of default parameter set: KWKV1.1 Luft-Wasser-Wärmepumpe (dezentral) - 20 kW_th

short_description: Enter the coefficient of performance, i.e. heat output per unit of electricity input, e.g. 3,5 as a constant value or, as a timeseries, one value per hour, e.g. as an Excel file with two columns (A: hour 1–8.760, B: COP) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;3,2).
rtd_description: The coefficient of performance (COP) is the ratio of heat output to electricity input of the heat pump. It depends strongly on the temperature of the heat source and the required supply temperature: an air source heat pump reaches a high COP in mild weather and a low COP on cold days, while ground source heat pumps operate more evenly. A constant value, e.g. the seasonal performance factor, is sufficient for a first estimate; for more realistic results, a COP timeseries with one value per hour can be uploaded, which can be calculated from temperature data e.g. with oemof.thermal. The number of values must match the scenario settings (8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps), and the file structure is the same as for all timeseries: an Excel file with two columns (A: hour or timestamp, B: COP) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;3,2). The parameters of the heat pump refer to its nominal heat output.

Provide the PV generation per 1 kWp of installed capacity as one value between 0 and 1 per hour, e.g. as an Excel file with two columns (A: hour 1–8.760, B: value in kW/kWp) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;0,45).
rtd_description: The timeseries describes the PV generation per 1 kWp of installed capacity in each hour, i.e. a value between 0 and 1 in kW/kWp. The size of the plant is not part of the timeseries but is entered separately as installed capacity or determined by the optimization; the tool multiplies both, e.g. a value of 0,45 for a plant with 100 kWp results in 45 kW in that hour. This separation allows the optimization to test different plant sizes with the same weather-based profile. The number of values must match the scenario settings, i.e. 8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps, and the first value belongs to the start date of the simulation. The data can be uploaded as an Excel file with two columns, in which column A contains the hour number (1 to 8.760) or a timestamp and column B the values; a header row is allowed, but empty cells are not. Alternatively, a CSV file without header can be used, either with one column containing only the values or with two columns separated by a semicolon (e.g. 1;0,45). Suitable values can be downloaded from Renewables.ninja with a capacity of 1 kW and the tilt and orientation of the planned installation, whose CSV export contains metadata and header lines at the top that have to be removed first, or calculated from measured data by dividing each hourly value by the nominal capacity, e.g. 45 kWh / 100 kWp = 0,45. As a plausibility check, no value may exceed 1, and the sum of all values gives the annual full load hours, typically about 900 to 1.100 h for PV in Germany.

During operation, it takes solar irradiance as its primary input and, through the photovoltaic effect in semiconductor solar cells, converts it into electrical energy. This process is mainly governed by the timeseries parameter, which defines the specific power output per kWp of installed capacity in each timestep and thus also reflects the orientation and tilt of the chosen installation type. \n\nSource of default parameter set: DEATechnikKatalogEl_andDh - 08.26 - PV - solar- residential rooftop - 0,006 MW_el per unit -ctrl. 2025

rtd_description: The Commodity component is used to supply an energy carrier, such as natural gas or wood, from outside the system boundary. During operation, it takes no physical input from within the system and, through a purchase from an external market, supplies the commodity to the connected bus. This process is mainly governed by the variable costs parameter, which defines the price per kWh of the commodity, while the optional nominal capacity and maximum annual full load hours limit the available supply. Energy can only be purchased via this component; selling or feeding energy back requires an energy provider (DSO) component.

rtd_description: The nominal capacity defines the maximum power at which the commodity can be supplied in each timestep, e.g. the capacity of a gas connection or the maximum delivery rate of a supplier. It is also the reference for the maximum annual full load hours. If no value is given, the supply is unlimited.

rtd_description: The maximum annual full load hours limit the total energy flow over the simulated period to the given number of hours multiplied by the nominal capacity, e.g. 2.000 h for a 100 kW component allow at most 200.000 kWh. The hours do not have to be consecutive; the optimization decides when the component operates. This can represent a limited annual supply, e.g. of wood or biogas, or a limited annual consumption or contract volume. For simulation periods shorter than one year, the value refers to the simulated period.

Prices given per volume or mass have to be converted with the calorific value, e.g. 1,70 € per litre of heating oil with about 10 kWh per litre correspond to 0,17 €/kWh.

It can be used for consumers with a permanent base load. As the model is linear, the sink cannot be switched off completely while a minimum is set. rtd_description: The maximum operation level defines the upper limit of the flow in every timestep as a factor of the nominal capacity, e.g. 0,8 for a 100 kW sink means a consumption of at most 80 kW in every hour. It can be used if a consumer can only use part of its nominal power, e.g. due to technical or contractual restrictions. The maximum can also be given as a timeseries with one value per hour, e.g. 1 during operating hours and 0 at night for a neighbouring company that only takes heat while it is operating; the number of values must match the scenario settings (8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps), and the file structure is the same as for all timeseries: an Excel file with two columns (A: hour or timestamp, B: value) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;0,8). A maximum cannot be combined with a fixed operation profile; without a value, the full nominal capacity is available in every hour.

short_description: Enter a fixed operation profile relative to the nominal capacity: one value between 0 and 1 per hour, e.g. as an Excel file with two columns (A: hour 1–8.760, B: value) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;0,5). Use either fix or minimum/maximum, not both.
rtd_description: The fixed operation profile defines the flow of the sink in every timestep as a factor of the nominal capacity, so the optimization can only decide on the size of the sink but not on its operation. It is useful if the shape of the consumption profile is known but its size is to be optimized. Like the generation profiles of PV or wind, the values are given per 1 kW of nominal capacity, i.e. between 0 and 1, and the tool multiplies them with the installed or optimized capacity, e.g. a value of 0,5 for a 100 kW sink means a consumption of 50 kW in that hour. The number of values must match the scenario settings (8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps), and the file structure is the same as for all timeseries: an Excel file with two columns (A: hour or timestamp, B: value) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;0,5). A fixed profile cannot be combined with a minimum or maximum operation level; either the exact profile is given with fix, or a corridor is defined with minimum and maximum.

It represents technical ramp limits, e.g. of industrial processes that cannot change their consumption abruptly. Without a value, the flow can change freely.

It represents technical ramp limits, e.g. of processes that have to be shut down slowly. Without a value, the flow can change freely.

This can represent a limited annual supply, e.g. of wood or biogas, or a limited annual consumption or contract volume. They depend on the pipe length, diameter and insulation as well as on the temperature difference between the heat carrier and the ground, and therefore increase with higher supply temperatures. As these losses also occur in hours with low heat demand, they are particularly relevant in summer. Instead of a constant value, the losses can also be given as a timeseries with one value per hour, e.g. to consider higher losses in winter, when the supply temperature is higher and the ground is colder. The number of values must match the scenario settings (8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps), and the file structure is the same as for all timeseries: an Excel file with two columns (A: hour or timestamp, B: losses) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;50); the values have to be given in the same unit as the constant value.

rtd_description: The Energy Bus component is used to connect all producers, consumers, storages and conversion components that exchange the same energy carrier, such as electricity, heat, gas or hydrogen. During operation, it takes the energy flows of all connected components as its input and, through an energy balance in every timestep (total incoming energy equals total outgoing energy, valid for all bus types), distributes them to the connected outputs without losses. This process is mainly governed by the balanced bus parameter, which defines whether supply and demand must be equal in every timestep, together with the excess and shortage energy costs that penalize any imbalance. Surplus and missing energy are handled by the Excess and Shortage components, which belong to the bus and are described below.

short_description: Select the energy carrier that is transported on this bus, e.g. electricity, gas, heat or hydrogen.
Decide whether supply and demand on this bus must be balanced in every timestep.
rtd_description: A balanced bus enforces the energy balance equation in every timestep: the sum of all incoming flows equals the sum of all outgoing flows. This is the normal setting for all buses. If the bus is not balanced, energy may appear or disappear on the bus without any cost, which usually leads to unrealistic results; it should therefore only be switched off for testing purposes or special modelling cases. Intended imbalances, such as surplus generation or unmet demand, are better represented by the excess and shortage energy costs.

short_description: Enter the penalty per kWh of excess energy that cannot be used, or leave empty to forbid excess energy.
rtd_description: The excess energy cost defines the penalty per kWh of energy that is produced but can neither be used, stored nor fed into a grid and is therefore dumped. In the open-plan-tool, an excess sink is placed automatically on each energy bus, assuming sufficient vents (heat) or resistors (electricity) to dump excess generation. With a cost of 0, excess energy is allowed without penalty; this is mainly relevant when non-dispatchable sources such as PV or wind are present, as dispatchable sources are not operated beyond the demand because of their costs. A positive value makes the optimization avoid excess energy, e.g. by choosing smaller generators or larger storages. If no value is given on the bus, excess energy is not permitted at all, which can make the optimization infeasible if the generation cannot be reduced. Very high excess energy indicates an oversized system and makes the results unrealistic.

short_description: Enter the penalty per kWh of unmet demand, or leave empty to forbid shortage energy.
rtd_description: The shortage energy cost defines the penalty per kWh of demand that cannot be covered by the available components. It is a virtual cost that does not represent real payments, but tells the optimization how severe an unmet demand is compared to investing in additional capacity. A very high value, such as the default of 10.000 €/kWh on the bus, practically forbids shortages, while a lower value can be used to deliberately allow a limited supply gap, e.g. to analyse the value of lost load. A value of 0 would allow unmet demand free of charge and should therefore be avoided. If no value is given on the bus, shortage energy is not permitted, which can make the optimization infeasible if the demand cannot be covered. As the open-plan-tool assumes no shortage or grid interruption in the system, any shortage in the results should be checked carefully.

short_description: The default values represent empirical data.
rtd_description: The Heating Pipe component is used to connect two heat buses, for example two sections of a heating network or two buildings, and to transport thermal energy between them. During operation, it takes heat from the first connected heat bus as its primary input and, through the flow of hot water in an insulated pipe, delivers it to the second heat bus, optionally in both directions. This process is mainly governed by the relative and absolute heat losses parameters, which define the share and the amount of heat lost during transport.

short_description: Select the first heat bus the pipe is connected to.
Select the second heat bus the pipe is connected to.
Enter the heat losses of the pipe per timestep.
rtd_description: The absolute heat losses describe the heat lost to the surroundings in each timestep, independent of the amount of transported heat, as the pipes are kept at operating temperature. They depend on the pipe length, diameter and insulation as well as on the temperature difference between the heat carrier and the ground, and therefore increase with higher supply temperatures. As these losses also occur in hours with low heat demand, they are particularly relevant in summer.

short_description: Enter the heat losses per timestep as a factor of the transferred heat, e.g. 0,1 for 10%.
rtd_description: The relative heat losses describe the share of the transported heat that is lost during transport, e.g. 0,1 means that 90 kWh arrive at the second bus when 100 kWh are fed in. Unlike the absolute losses, they increase with the amount of transported heat. Typical annual heat losses of district heating networks are in the range of about 10 to 20 % of the heat fed in.

short_description: Decide whether the pipe can transport heat in both directions.
rtd_description: If the return pipe option is activated, heat can be transported in both directions between the two connected heat buses, e.g. if heat generators are located on both sides of the pipe. Otherwise, heat only flows from the first to the second heat bus.

rtd_description: The DSO Hydrogen component is used to connect the energy system to an external hydrogen supply, such as a hydrogen pipeline network or a supplier, allowing hydrogen to be purchased and surplus hydrogen to be sold. During operation, it takes hydrogen from the external supply as its primary input and, through the supply connection, delivers it to the connected hydrogen bus, while surplus hydrogen can flow in the opposite direction. This process is mainly governed by the energy price and feed-in tariff parameters, which define the costs and revenues per kWh of exchanged hydrogen.

Enter the price per kWh paid for energy drawn from the grid, e.g. 0,30 as a constant price. Only a constant value can be entered for this provider.
rtd_description: The energy price is the price per kWh of the energy carrier sourced from the provider. It should include all cost components that depend on the consumed energy, such as procurement, energy-related grid fees, taxes and levies, as far as they are relevant for the project. For this provider, the energy price can only be entered as a constant value, e.g. an average annual price; time-dependent prices can currently only be uploaded for the electricity provider. Capacity-related grid fees are entered separately as peak demand pricing.

rtd_description: The feed-in tariff is the price received per kWh fed into the grid of the provider. The feed-in is represented by a feed-in sink, able to take in generation that is provided to the energy provider for revenue. For this provider, the feed-in tariff can only be entered as a constant value; it must not be higher than the energy price, otherwise the tool reports an error, as the optimization could buy and sell energy at the same time without limit. The amount of feed-in can be limited with the maximum feed-in power.

It should include all cost components that depend on the consumed energy, such as procurement, energy-related grid fees, taxes and levies, as far as they are relevant for the project. Instead of a constant value, energy prices can be added as values that vary over time, e.g. hourly market prices for a dynamic tariff. Such a timeseries contains absolute prices in €/kWh, one value per hour, and the first value belongs to the start date of the simulation; the number of values must match the scenario settings (8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps), and the file structure is the same as for all timeseries: an Excel file with two columns (A: hour or timestamp, B: price in €/kWh) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;0,30). Please make sure that the prices are given in €/kWh and as hourly values. Capacity-related grid fees are entered separately as peak demand pricing.

Like the energy price, it can be given as a timeseries, e.g. for direct marketing at market prices, with one value in €/kWh per hour; the number of values must match the scenario settings (8.760 values for 365 days with 60-minute timesteps), and the file structure is the same as for all timeseries: an Excel file with two columns (A: hour or timestamp, B: tariff in €/kWh) or a CSV file without header (e.g. 1;0,08). The feed-in tariff must not be higher than the energy price in any hour, otherwise the tool reports an error, as the optimization could buy and sell energy at the same time without limit. The amount of feed-in can be limited with the maximum feed-in power.

rtd_description: The Energy Excess component belongs to an energy bus and is used to absorb surplus energy on a bus that can neither be consumed, stored nor fed into a grid, so that the energy balance of the bus is always maintained. In the open-plan-tool, an excess sink is added automatically to every energy bus, assuming that the surplus can always be dissipated, for heat e.g. to the environment and for electricity e.g. via load resistors. During operation, it takes the excess energy of the connected bus as its primary input and, through a virtual sink, removes it from the system without further use. This process is mainly governed by the excess energy cost parameter, which defines the penalty per kWh of dumped energy and thus whether and how strongly the optimization avoids excess energy.

short_description: Enter the penalty per kWh of excess energy on the bus, e.g. 0 to allow surplus energy to be dumped free of charge.

A positive value makes the optimization avoid excess energy, e.g. by choosing smaller generators or larger storages. If no value is given on the bus, excess energy is not permitted at all, which can make the optimization infeasible if the generation cannot be reduced. Very high excess energy indicates an oversized system and makes the results unrealistic.

short_description: asset_name
rtd_description: The Energy Shortage component belongs to an energy bus and is used to cover demand on a bus that cannot be met by the available production, storage or supply components, so that the energy balance of the system can always be met. During operation, it takes no physical input and, through a virtual source, feeds the missing energy into the connected bus. This process is mainly governed by the shortage energy cost parameter, which defines the penalty per kWh of unmet demand and thus how strongly the optimization avoids supply gaps.
